articles.title: Natalie Wood's daughter confronts very painful way she learned Hollywood icon had died at 11
articles.summary: Natasha Gregson Wagner describes the childhood sleepover that shattered her world when she learned Natalie Wood had died off Catalina Island.
articles.body: Natasha Gregson Wagner was just 11 years old when an ordinary childhood sleepover turned into a moment that shattered her world. While staying at a friend's house, she heard the devastating news on the radio: her mother, Hollywood actress Natalie Wood, was dead. "As a child, I always knew my mom was home because her Jungle Gardenia scent arrived before she did," Gregson Wagner, now 56, wrote on the website for her fragrance brand, L'Amour Mere. "After she died, I spent hours lying in her bed or sitting in her closet among her clothes. If I could somehow keep her fragrance alive, perhaps she would not be entirely gone." CHARLIZE THERON RECOUNTS THE NIGHT HER MOTHER FATALLY SHOT HER FATHER WHEN SHE WAS 15 YEARS OLD In the immediate aftermath of Wood's death, Gregson Wagner said the two father figures in her life — her biological father, British film producer Richard Gregson, and her stepfather, actor Robert Wagner — came together to support her. "Luckily, I had these two men, Daddy Gregson and Daddy Wagner, who came together and rose to the occasion and completely put me first," Gregson Wagner told the Daily Mail. "They got me into therapy right away, and I had that same amazing therapist here in Beverly Hills until my 20s." Wood, who was nominated for three Oscars and starred in "West Side Story" and "Rebel Without a Cause," was on the family's yacht with Wagner, actor Christopher Walken and captain Dennis Davern during Thanksgiving weekend in 1981. Her body was found floating in the water off Southern California's Catalina Island. She was 43. WATCH: ROBERT WAGNER'S MOST MEMORABLE ROLES, FROM ‘HART TO HART’ TO ‘AUSTIN POWERS’ Investigators initially ruled Wood's death an accidental drowning but reopened the case in 2011 to determine whether Wagner or anyone else played a role after the yacht's captain said he heard the couple arguing the night of her disappearance, The Associated Press reported. The Los Angeles County coroner's office amended Wood's death certificate in 2012, changing the cause of death to "drowning and other undetermined factors." In 2018, Los Angeles County sheriff's investigators described Wagner as "a person of interest" in Wood's death. In 2022, the department said it had exhausted all leads in the case, and Wagner was no longer considered a person of interest. Wagner has long denied having any involvement in his wife's death. Gregson Wagner said that while she was growing up, her two fathers were determined to give her a normal upbringing away from the glaring media spotlight. "I had to do my laundry," she told the outlet. "We had dinner on the table at six o'clock. I learned how to cook in their kitchen. I learned how to do laundry. I learned how to take a bath with a hot tap and a cold tap, putting it in a pot and pouring it on my head and all these things." Gregson Wagner also told the outlet she avoided the drugs and alcohol that have troubled some children of famous parents. "I've definitely felt pressure in my life," Gregson Wagner said. "I know what's right, I know what's wrong. I'm not saying I haven't had very, very painful things in my life.... But in the home, it was all very safe and secure and warm. So, I got lucky in that way." LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS Still, Gregson Wagner said she continues to feel the impact of losing her mother. "When I was younger, I would get stopped on the street by people who would say things like: 'You look so much like this actress, you've probably never heard of her, but her name was Natalie Wood,'" Gregson Wagner recalled. "Most of the time I wouldn't admit I was her daughter, and just say: 'Oh, I hear that a lot!'" "We looked so much alike and had so much in common. Where did the mother end and the child begin? We were so completely connected — and she was so sharp and perceptive — that I sometimes believed she could see right into my mind." Gregson Wagner has been married to "7th Heaven" alum Barry Watson, 52, since 2014. They share a daughter, Clover. Gregson Wagner also launched the fragrance brand L'Amour Mere, which she says was inspired by her mother and their connection through scent. Gregson Wagner has previously spoken about her mother's legacy. In 2020, Gregson Wagner appeared in the HBO documentary "Natalie Wood: What Remains Behind," which featured interviews with Wood's family, close friends and confidants. Wagner, now 96, also appeared in the documentary and discussed his relationship with Wood and her death. The couple married in 1957 but divorced in 1962. They remarried in 1972 and were together until Wood's passing. Wagner helped raise Gregson Wagner, and he and Wood had a daughter, Courtney Wagner, who also appeared in the documentary. "I am always blown away by his courage," Gregson Wagner told Fox News Digital at the time. "As my dad and knowing him for basically my whole life, I know him to be such a courageous person. I was just so proud of him. I felt like he was so transparent, elegant, gracious, emotional, connected and present. He was everything that I know him to be, so it felt like an incredible experience to bear witness as his daughter. He's one of the great loves of my life. He moves me every day, and he deeply moved me on those days [of filming] for sure." Gregson Wagner said she still has vivid, joyful memories of Wood. "My mom made being a mom feel really effortless," Gregson Wagner said. "She loved it so much. She was always singing songs with us. We were always painting and reading. She was always there to talk to. I hear her voice a lot when I talk to [my daughter] Clover. Like, 'What are we going to do today? Are we going to take a walk?' Just the little mundane things. I can hear her voice in my ear when I talk to my own daughter." "My parents wanted their children to have that constant feeling of being loved and nurtured — the joy of childhood," she continued. "And that's what they did. Friends came over all the time and sometimes they went out. But the focus was really on us. I think we felt really safe in their world and around them. They were able to create just a bustling, joyful, jubilant kind of atmosphere for us to grow up." She said the special was ultimately a celebration of Wood's life and what she accomplished both in Hollywood and as a parent. During a conversation at the Pendulum Summit in Dublin in 2019, a question about his love life led Farrell to share something much bigger about the way he looks at life.Today’s quote of the day by Colin Farrell reads: “I love life. I grab it by the horns and knock it out of the arena.”What does the quote by Colin Farrell mean?Farrell’s words show someone who does not want to simply sit back and let life pass by. When he talks about grabbing life “by the horns,” Farrell is basically saying that he wants to live fully, take chances and make the most of what comes his way.The comment came during Farrell’s conversation with journalist Miriam O’Callaghan at the Pendulum Summit in Dublin in 2019. When O’Callaghan asked him about his love life, Farrell initially tried to move away from the topic. But when she asked again, he replied, “Oh, I love life. I do love it. I grab it by the horns and knock it out of the arena.” The exchange was reported by The Irish Times.What makes the moment interesting is that Farrell did not simply give an answer about romance. Instead, he turned the conversation toward his relationship with life itself. His words suggest that enjoying life can sometimes come from being willing to take chances, staying open to new experiences and making the most of the time you have.Why does his message still matter today?It’s easy to relate to what Farrell is saying when your mind is always on the next thing you have to do. Work, deadlines and personal plans can keep you busy, and before you know it, you may forget to slow down and enjoy what’s happening around you. His words are a reminder that you don’t need to have your whole life planned out before you can enjoy it. Plans can change, things can go wrong, and unexpected opportunities can appear. None of that necessarily means there is nothing to look forward to.There is also something relatable about the way Farrell puts it. He does not describe life as perfect or easy. When you look at Farrell’s own life, those words feel even more personal. His career has brought major successes, while his personal life has also had its share of difficult periods. His quote therefore feels less like a simple motivational line and more like a reflection of the way he chooses to approach life.Early life of Colin FarrellColin Farrell was born in Castleknock, Dublin, in 1976. Acting was not always the obvious path for him. He grew up in a family with strong sporting connections, with his father, Eamon Farrell, and uncle Tommy Farrell both having played football for Shamrock Rovers.Farrell eventually became interested in acting and attended the Gaiety School of Acting in Dublin. He did not complete the course, however, as acting opportunities began arriving before he could finish his studies. One of his early television roles came in the BBC series 'Ballykissangel'.How did Colin Farrell rise to fame?Farrell's career began moving forward when he started taking on film roles. Farrell made his film debut in 'The War Zone' in 1999. A year later, he took on the lead role in Joel Schumacher’s 'Tigerland'. The role gave him a much bigger opportunity and helped put him on Hollywood’s radar.More major roles followed, including 'Minority Report', 'Phone Booth' and 'Daredevil'. Over time, Farrell also took on very different kinds of characters, from mainstream Hollywood roles to more independent films. His performance in 'In Bruges' later earned him a Golden Globe for Best Actor in a Musical or Comedy.His career has continued to move between different genres and styles rather than following one fixed path. Looking back at that journey, Farrell’s words about loving life feel particularly fitting. His story itself has involved unexpected turns, new opportunities and plenty of change.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: Are you ready for everything to look like TikTok?
articles.summary: Meta is testing making Facebook and Instagram open directly into full screen vertical video feeds, just like TikTok. It offers a preview of what all social media could come to look like.
articles.body: Since TikTok burst into mainstream consciousness, many things have been called a “TikTok clone”: YouTube Shorts, Instagram Reels, Snapchat Spotlight, Netflix’s Clips, LinkedIn’s vertical video feed, and countless other, less recognizable names like Triller, Zynn, and Byte. For years now, Facebook and Instagram have pumped users’ feeds with video as Meta chases TikTok’s runaway success. But if tests running abroad are any indication, the TikTok-ification of social media might finally be reaching its fullest form. TechCrunch reports that some users in India are getting a Facebook test that, upon opening the app, drops them directly into an immersive, full-screen video feed. Meta hinted that this “experience” would be coming to “video-heavy countries” first, followed by a potential US expansion in 2027. At the same time, Romania-based app researcher Radu Oncescu noticed an option on Instagram to have Reels be the first thing a user sees when they open the app. Instagram Stories remain at the top of the feed, per screenshots from Oncescu, while swiping the screen pulls up the traditional feed of posts from accounts a user follows. Sound is on for Reels by default. Meta spokesperson Devi Narasimhan told The Verge that the Instagram test is live in a handful of countries, but didn’t specify which. Users can switch back to the original layout, Narasimhan says, and Reels will be unmuted once a user swipes or clicks into a video. [Media: There’s still a chance Instagram and Facebook won’t end up looking exactly like TikTok — not all tests become permanent features. But we have been barreling toward this for a long time, with some user pushback along the way that always seems to get ironed out. Video content made for quick consumption is clearly a priority for Meta. Even Threads, Meta’s text-based platform that reaches half a billion people every month, was barely mentioned in the company’s recent earnings call. What was mentioned? Time users spent watching videos on Facebook (up 9 percent globally and 10 percent in the US and Canada), improvements to the ranking system used for Reels, and ranking models that the company says can “identify high-quality new Reels at creation.” TikTok’s — and by extension, its copycats’ — focus on video has reshaped all of the industries that depend upon such platforms for distribution. Podcasts have become videos, which have become clips. TV shows have become “microdramas” and movies have been chopped up into 50 parts. Political astroturfing has taken on the form of “user-generated content.” It’s not clear if users actually prefer video over text or images, or if they simply engage with it because it’s what social media platforms have placed directly in front of them — engagement is engagement, so platforms likely don’t care either way. But as social media has turned video-focused, users report posting less online. Morning Consult polling found that while 81 percent of US respondents reported watching an Instagram Reel, only 39 percent say they’ve posted one. What happens when watching videos is the backbone of what we do online, yet relatively few people want to make them in the first place? This explains, at least in part, why platforms tolerate or even recommend AI slop content. Whether a slowdown in posting is because of the move to video is anyone’s guess, but it’s clear we have all become voyeurs. The potential for Instagram and Facebook to become video feeds by default would be a seismic shift in form. But it would also mark the end of a more philosophical distinction: that these platforms are for keeping in touch with people. It was painful enough to ask writers, photographers, nonprofits, podcasters, and other creatives to spin up video content studios just to avoid being rendered invisible by the algorithm. It’s another to ask your aunt and old college roommate to do the same or get bumped onto a different page, easily forgotten. Time will tell if engagement is high enough for Meta to go forward with these tests in the US and other regions. If and when it does expand, at least we will have seen it coming.

articles.title: Ben Affleck is an AI nerd, and the internet is impressed | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Ben Affleck is going viral for his deep knowledge of AI, from neural networks and transformers to open weights. The actor, who sold his AI filmmaking startup to Netflix earlier this year, is proving he's more than just a Hollywood star.
articles.body:
They cast the wrong lead in “Good Will Hunting,” apparently, because it’s Ben Affleck who is the secret genius, as it turns out. The actor who earlier this year sold his AI filmmaking startup to Netflix for a reported $587 million has gone viral this week for demonstrating his understanding of AI technology, neural networks, machine learning, and the like, across multiple video clips of his recent interviews.

He can even write a little Python, he says.

The movie star delved into his interest in technology most recently on an episode of GQ’s “One More Question” series this week, where he humbly started with “I’ve always been kind of into computers since I was young,” before nerding out on the development of AI as it relates to filmmaking, while using AI terminology like machine learning, neural networks, transformers, tensors, GPUs, inference, and more.

In a clip that’s making the rounds, Affleck explains to the impressed interviewer, Zach Baron, that he got into the space when analog film moved to digital. As he spoke, he kept defining terms so the interviewer could understand what he was talking about.

“I became more interested in that aspect of it, and the visual effects workflow for many years has included machine learning,” Affleck began. “So I can write, like, pretty shitty Python scripts and stuff like that. Because with convolutional neural networks — which were the sort of precursors to what the transformer can do — which is just much more computation simultaneously — you would do things like, look at what’s called a tensor — which is just the numerical translation of a visual image, in numbers like the batch number, the frame number, the red, green, and blue values of each pixel in each frame, and how many? It’s just that simple, right?”

No, Ben Affleck, it is not just that simple, which is why this video is going viral.

The actor then went into how neural networks were used to identify patterns and do edge detection or feature extraction, which he described as “identifying patterns enough to know — like this is where the window ledge is, so we can more easily take the green screen image out and replace it with something.”

He also admitted he used his status as a Hollywood star to get a peek at emerging AI technology, at times. OpenAI was among those he visited, Affleck said in a separate clip, which ultimately led him to understand how he could get more directly involved in the AI space.

As the interviewer continued, Affleck explained how AI can help with filmmaking while not replacing it, leading to the development and sale of his own startup in this space. (He claims the $587 million figure is “not right,” noting that he didn’t own the whole company.)

“I gambled on this notion that in order to do this in an ethical way and in a way that could take this technology and actually make it work hand in glove with artists in this community where there are very fixed, long-standing relationships around likeness and so forth, we had to create our own dataset,” he said. “So I raised the money. I shot for about eight months with a lot of cameras and a lot of equipment, and created a dataset that would serve as late-stage training for open models to do discrete tasks, sort of where the training code, the inference code, were related to one another and geared toward actual specific tasks that would generate value,” Affleck said.

In a separate clip, also going viral, Affleck spoke to Bloomberg’s Lucas Shaw at the Screentime 2026 conference in LA, where he talked about how he fine-tuned AI models by taking open source models, unfreezing the weights, then teaching them to meet certain cinematic standards. In the process, the filmmaker retains their proprietary work, while benefiting from the learning they create by training their own unique model for the movie they’re making.

The actor used the technique himself in his movie “Animals,” where AI aided in the post-production process.

At one point, he also weighed in on the concerns around AI and its world-ending potential . His worries, however, were much more rational.

“When I worry about AI, I worry about my kids in school. I worry about the 30% rise in the number of A’s given out at colleges over the last three years. I worry about learned helplessness. I worry about responsible use. I don’t worry about Skynet, and I don’t think that it’s going to take over [the movie] business in any meaningful way. I think it’s going to be additive,” Affleck said.

articles.title: Israeli actress calls out Hollywood stars 'silencing artists' who support Jewish state
articles.summary: Noa Cohen pushed back against Hollywood celebrities calling for boycotts of Israeli film institutions, saying "silencing artists" closes conversation.
articles.body: Israeli actress Noa Cohen pushed back against celebrities "silencing artists" supporting the Jewish state, according to comments reported by The Hollywood Reporter Wednesday. Cohen spoke to The Hollywood Reporter about her latest film, "Our Loves," a drama set during the deadly Oct. 7 terror attacks in 2023. The film, one of the first to dramatize the events, drew criticism for being told largely through Israeli citizens' perspectives as Hollywood stars continue to speak out against Israel. The 24-year-old actress, who knew many victims of the Hamas attacks, expressed dismay at celebrities' actions, particularly their calls to boycott Israeli film institutions. COMEDIAN DECLARES JERRY SEINFELD 'UNCANCELLABLE' DESPITE 'WOKE' ANTI-ISRAEL FESTIVAL BOYCOTT "Silencing artists because of government policies closes conversation. And don’t we need to keep that open?" Cohen said. In 2025, over 1,000 Hollywood stars, directors and other film workers, including Emma Stone and Mark Ruffalo, signed a pledge to boycott institutions such as festivals, cinemas, broadcasters and production companies that "are implicated in genocide and apartheid against the Palestinian people." Cohen denied films like "Our Loves" erased the Palestinian people and encouraged a more open mind. HOLLYWOOD STARS LIKE MAYIM BIALIK, DEBRA MESSING AMONG 1,200 BLASTING ISRAELI FILM BOYCOTT AS 'ERASURE OF ART' "I mean, you don’t have to agree with a government to hear the stories of its people," Cohen said. In the meantime, she told The Hollywood Reporter she and several others are still grieving the losses of that day. "You couldn’t really grieve until all the hostages were home," Cohen said. "So, really, we’re not even at the end of the first year of grieving. And there will be many more years." 'NOBODY WANTS THIS': CONSULTING RABBI CALLS OUT STAR'S 'IGNORANT' TAKE ON 'GENOCIDE' IN GAZA Cohen is perhaps best known for her portrayal as the Virgin Mary in Netflix's "Mary," which premiered in 2024. At the time, Cohen's casting caused an uproar among anti-Israel critics for casting an Israeli woman in the role, insisting that the real Mary was "Palestinian." The film's director, D.J. Caruso, previously defended the casting in a statement, saying, "It was important to us that Mary, along with most of our primary cast, be selected from Israel to ensure authenticity." In a comment to Fox News Digital, the Israeli-American Council (IAC) stood by Cohen's comments and called out efforts to target Israeli institutions and citizens. But freedom of speech does not mean freedom to apply a double standard and engage in discrimination," the IAC said. "There is a clear difference between criticizing Israel's government policies and targeting Israeli artists because of their faith or national origin. Boycotting Israeli artists in the name of artistic freedom is disingenuous, wrong and a clear act of antisemitism."

articles.body: Kolhapur: For nearly three decades, Gangavesh resident Amar Jadhav carried a friendship that most fans can only dream of. What began as a chance meeting with actor Nana Patekar at Kolhapur’s Rankala lake during the shooting of ‘Yugpurush’ in 1997 blossomed into a bond that transcended celebrity and fandom.Now 60, Jadhav remembers not the cinematic genius, but the mentor, guide and friend who opened his doors and heart to him. “When I told Nana sir how big a fan I was, he invited me to his Mumbai home for the Ganesh festival. That visit turned into a tradition that continued since then,” Jadhav recalled, fighting back emotions before rushing to Donje for the actor’s last rites.Their relationship evolved into social work. Through Nana Patekar Vichar Manch, they championed girls’ education and launched an initiative to create a Rs 5,000 fixed deposit for every girl child born on Jan 1, Patekar’s birthday.The actor’s generosity often arrived without fanfare. When Patekar learnt that the ambulance operated by Jadhav’s organisation had fallen into disrepair, he immediately stepped in. “Within no time, he arranged a brand-new ambulance for us,” Jadhav said.The bond extended deep into family life. During the Covid-19 pandemic, when travel restrictions prevented him from attending Jadhav’s daughter’s wedding, Patekar joined through a video call to personally bless the bride. “He knew every member of my family. Sometimes he would call and ask for Kolhapuri jaggery. I would personally take it to Mumbai, because it gave me another chance to meet my hero,” Jadhav said.Kolhapur, too, held a special place in Patekar’s heart. Some of his early films, including ‘Bhalu’, were shot at the now-defunct Jayprabha Studio. Despite achieving national fame, he never forgot the city that shaped part of his artistic journey.His support for Kolhapur’s cultural institutions was unwavering too. He donated Rs 5 lakh to Gayan Samaj Deval Club during its 125th foundation anniversary celebrations and remained closely connected with the city’s artistic fraternity. But perhaps the moment that best captured the man behind the actor came after the 26/11 Mumbai terror attacks. While in Kolhapur, Patekar was invited to speak at a public event. He declined the microphone. articles.title: ‘Nana inhabited every role’: Friends remember a restless actor shaped by Marathi theatre
articles.summary: Friends and colleagues recall Nana Patekar’s journey from Marathi theatre to iconic films like Natsamrat, praising his grit, humility, and role immersion.
articles.body: Pune: Long before his voice could slice through silence and his intensity could own the screen, Nana Patekar was a restless young actor fighting for space on the Marathi stage. Those who knew him then don’t remember a star in the making, just a hungry performer driven by instinct, grit and stubborn commitment to his craft.Veteran actor Ashok Saraf recalled those early days with a mixture of affection and admiration. When Patekar first walked into Hamidabaichi Kothi, Anil Barve’s celebrated play directed by Vijaya Mehta, he was still inexperienced. But slowly, scene by scene, performance by performance, Patekar seized the stage and made it his own.“He started with acting and never looked back. He was good to those who were good to him and tough with those who were not. I can never forget him,” Saraf recalled.Their friendship was forged in hard times. Saraf earned Rs 250 per show while Patekar earned Rs 50. Between rehearsals, they passed hours playing cards to distract themselves from an uncertain future. When Patekar hit serious financial trouble, Saraf silently gave him a blank cheque and said, “Withdraw whatever you need from the Rs 15,000 in my account.” Patekar withdrew Rs 3,000.Years later, when he returned the money, Saraf joked that success had finally made him wealthy. Patekar’s reply stayed with him forever: “I am returning only the money. I can never return the time you gave me.”That was Patekar. Fiercely independent, deeply grateful and never one to forget those who stood by him.His years under theatre legend Vijaya Mehta shaped his understanding of acting. He learnt that a character’s true drama lies not in dialogue but in the conflicts simmering beneath it. That lesson stayed with him when he made his film debut with ‘Gaman’ in 1978.Whether portraying an outsider, a rebel, a police officer or a real-life figure, Patekar never merely performed roles. He searched for the human being behind them. That approach found its fullest expression in ‘Natsamrat’. As Ganpat Belwalkar, the aging theatre titan at the centre of VV Shirwadkar’s classic, Patekar delivered one of the defining performances of Marathi cinema. His portrayal of pride, loneliness, aging and loss felt so lived-in that it seemed less like acting and more like a man confronting the ghosts of an entire lifetime.Director Mahesh Manjrekar, who knew Patekar since their theatre days and later directed him in ‘Natsamrat’, spoke of the loss with visible emotion. “This is my biggest loss after my parents. We have lost two pillars of Marathi cinema, Vikram Gokhale and now Nana. I still cannot believe he is no more. I was hoping to work with him again, but could not find a subject worthy of his talent,” he said.From ‘Deool’ and ‘Pak Pak Pakaak’ to ‘Dr Prakash Baba Amte: The Real Hero’ and ‘Aapla Manus’, Patekar returned repeatedly to Marathi cinema, even after Hindi films had turned him into a national icon. His portrayal of Dr Prakash Amte was another example of a rare gift that defined his career — he did not impersonate people, he inhabited them.Actor-director Amol Palekar’s memories reveal another side of Patekar. He remembered long conversations at Mumbai’s Ravindra Natya Mandir, where the two friends would discuss acting, life and the endless process of self-discovery. To Palekar, Patekar was an artist who never stopped working on himself.Palekar said only a day and a half before his passing, Patekar had called him up, expressing regret for missing the opening of his new play. “When I heard the news this morning, I felt completely numb. I remember how Nana (Patekar) had once fought with me for a role in one of his films, such was his determination to take on the part and build it from within,” Palekar said.“He was an extraordinarily gifted actor. He stood by me like a younger brother whenever I called,” Palekar added.Actor Sayaji Shinde struggled to process the news and remembered speaking to him only a day earlier. Beyond cinema, they worked together through NAAM Foundation, supporting farmers and drought-affected communities across Maharashtra. “We were talking so well yesterday and suddenly this happened. I do not know what to say. I kept wondering whether the news I was seeing was even true,” Shinde said.For singer Rahul Deshpande, Patekar was family. He spoke of Patekar’s affection for his grandfather and the way the actor later embraced him like a younger brother, offering guidance, encouragement and honest criticism. Patekar also took a personal interest in Deshpande’s Vasantotsav festival, pushing him to think bigger and international.“What many may not know is that Nana had an exceptionally sharp ear for music. Whether it was a ghazal, natyasangeet or a raga, his observations could be remarkably perceptive,” Deshpande said, adding, “The greatest lesson I learnt from Nana had little to do with music. It was about how to live. Despite everything he had achieved, there was no pretence about him. He remained simple, grounded and extraordinarily generous.”In many ways, Patekar never left the stage that shaped him. articles.title: This desktop Spotify alternative is less RAM hungry and supports Winamp skins.
articles.summary:
If you’re tired of the Spotify desktop app gobbling up a big chunk of your computer’s RAM, Spotifast for Linux, macOS, and Windows takes a leaner approach and typically needs just 100 to 250MB. A Spotify Premium account is required to actually stream music instead of just browsing, and if you need another reason to switch, Spotifast includes a Mini Player that supports Winamp 2 skins.
